claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA components can be produced by powder-based additive manufacturing followed by vacuum sintering.
Vacuum sintering around 1400 °C can substantially densify additively manufactured HfNbTaTiZr.
Slow cooling after sintering produces a multiphase microstructure in HfNbTaTiZr.
The slowly cooled multiphase microstructure is associated with residual stresses and fabrication defects.
An immediate post-sintering water quench will freeze a homogeneous, predominantly single-phase beta-BCC microstructure.
Water quenching will minimize grain growth and suppress brittle intermetallic phases.
Rapid quenching limits diffusion-driven phase transformations and grain coarsening by rapidly lowering temperature.
Suppressing multiphase evolution and microstructural defects decreases residual-stress buildup.
Decreasing residual-stress buildup will reduce dimensional distortion.
Water-quenched components will exhibit less shrinkage and warpage than conventionally slow-cooled components.
Water-quenched components will contain fewer fabrication-induced defects than conventionally slow-cooled components.
Water-quenched components will have higher yield strength than conventionally slow-cooled components.
Water-quenched components will have greater ductility than conventionally slow-cooled components.
Conventionally slow-cooled components develop higher residual thermal stresses and more pronounced dimensional inaccuracies.
The quench is expected to be most effective when the sintering temperature exceeds approximately 1400 °C and diffusion kinetics permit rapid phase freezing.
Large components may obtain diminished benefits because achieving uniform quench rates is difficult.
HEA compositions that inherently stabilize multiphase microstructures may obtain diminished benefits from water quenching.
The quantitative effects of water quenching on dimensional precision and mechanical properties in additive manufacturing have not been established and may depend on geometry and composition.
